lead: A Docker image packs your Express app, Node runtime and exact dependencies into one file. A container runs that image the same way on your laptop and on a cloud server. CI/CD turns a git push into install, test, build, push and deploy steps without a human copying files. This chapter shows the Dockerfile order that keeps builds fast, how secrets arrive as environment variables, the main cloud hosting choices, and a pipeline you can trace from push to a container listening on port 3000.
prereq: You need: 6.4 for the Express app being shipped and 6.2 for package.json, npm ci and scripts.

blocks.text: An image is a frozen file system plus a start command. A container is that image running as a process. The image is the recipe; the container is the cooked dish. One image can start many containers, like one class can create many objects. The same image behaves the same on a laptop and a cloud server because it carries Node and the exact packages from package-lock.json.
A Dockerfile lists instructions in order. Each instruction creates a layer, and Docker caches a layer until its inputs change. Read this file from top to bottom:

blocks.code:
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

blocks.text: FROM picks node:20-alpine as the base. WORKDIR /app makes /app the working directory. The first COPY brings only package.json and package-lock.json, so RUN npm ci is cached until those two files change. The second COPY brings your source code; editing server.js does not reinstall packages. EXPOSE 3000 documents the intended port. CMD is the foreground process that keeps the container alive. A .dockerignore file keeps node_modules, .git, .env and logs out of the image.

docker build -t shop . builds an image named shop from the current directory. docker run -p 8080:3000 shop maps host port 8080 to container port 3000. Host port comes first. Open http://localhost:8080; the app still listens on 3000 inside.

Passwords and database URLs are configuration, not code. Put them in environment variables at run time: docker run -e DATABASE_URL=... shop, or an env_file in Compose. Never write them in the Dockerfile or an ENV line; layers keep old values and anyone who pulls the image can read them.

Docker Compose describes several services in one YAML file. A typical file has app and db services: app builds from ., starts after db, and gets DATABASE_URL pointing at the service name db. Compose starts db before app, but does not wait for the database to be ready; add a health check with a depends_on condition, or make the app retry the connection. db uses a named volume so data survives a container restart. Compose creates one private network, so app reaches db by name, not by localhost.

items: IaaS: a VPS with root access; you install Docker and manage updates.
PaaS: a platform builds from your Git push and runs the container for you.
Managed database: the provider runs MySQL or MongoDB with backups and failover.
SaaS: ready software you use, not a place to deploy your code.

blocks.text: In production a reverse proxy such as Nginx listens on ports 80 and 443 and forwards requests to 127.0.0.1:3000. Keep port 3000 off the public internet. Logs go to three places: docker logs for app stdout/stderr, Nginx access.log and error.log for requests, and your cloud log viewer if the platform collects them.
CI/CD is one automatic path from commit to live container. A CI runner starts on every push.

items: Checkout the commit and run npm ci; it installs exactly package-lock.json, the same as local.
Run npm test. A failing test stops the pipeline before any image is built.
Build the image and tag it with the commit SHA: docker build -t registry.example.com/shop:${SHA} ..
Push that tag to a registry.
On the deploy host, pull the tag, inject environment variables, stop the old container, start the new one on port 3000, and check /health.
Keep the previous tag. If the health check fails, redeploy the previous tag: that is the rollback.

blocks.text: A tag like latest is not a version; the commit SHA is. A registry stores images (public or private), not source commits like a Git repository. One run takes install 40 s, test 25 s, build 30 s and deploy 15 s. A manual copy-and-restart can take 20 min.

examples.question: A shop API listens on port 3000 inside its container. Give the Dockerfile instruction order and the build and run commands to serve it on host port 8080. A CI run takes install 40 s, test 25 s, image build 30 s and deploy 15 s; manual deployment takes 20 min. Find total CI seconds and seconds saved.
steps: Dockerfile order: FROM node:20-alpine, WORKDIR /app, COPY package*.json ./, RUN npm ci, COPY . ., EXPOSE 3000, CMD ["node", "server.js"].
Run: docker run -p 8080:3000 shop. Host port 8080 comes first, container port 3000 second.
examples.answer: Total CI time is 110 s, and the saving is 1090 s (about 18 min 10 s).

traps: Writing COPY . . before RUN npm ci throws away the layer cache on every code change and reinstalls everything.
Reversing the port mapping: -p 3000:8080 is wrong when the app listens on 3000 and you want host 8080; use -p 8080:3000.
Putting passwords in the Dockerfile or an ENV line; they stay inside image layers even if a later line deletes them.
Thinking EXPOSE publishes the port. EXPOSE only documents it; docker run -p or Compose ports is needed.
Running a daemon in CMD such as a background process; when PID 1 exits, the container stops.

quiz.q: Define image and container. Which one is running?
quiz.a: An image is a frozen file system plus a start command. A container is that image running as a process.

quiz.q: Why does the Dockerfile copy package*.json before the source code?
quiz.a: So RUN npm ci is cached until package.json or package-lock.json changes. Source edits then reuse the installed node_modules layer.

quiz.q: An app listens on container port 3000. Write the command to expose it on host port 8080.
quiz.a: docker run -p 8080:3000 shop. Host port 8080 comes first; container port 3000 comes second.

quiz.q: npm test fails in the CI pipeline. What happens next, and why is that useful?
quiz.a: The pipeline stops before docker build and push. A broken commit never reaches the registry or deploy host, so production keeps the previous working tag.

quiz.q: A CI run takes install 50 s, test 20 s, build 40 s and deploy 10 s. Find the total seconds.
Why is a secret in a Dockerfile dangerous even if the next line deletes the file?
quiz.a: Each instruction is a layer. The secret remains in the earlier layer, and anyone who pulls the image can inspect layers and read it. Use run-time environment variables or a secret store.

quiz.q: What does Nginx do in front of an app on port 3000?
quiz.a: It listens on 80 and 443, forwards requests to 127.0.0.1:3000, handles TLS, and keeps port 3000 off the public internet.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production teams add health checks, blue-green and canary releases, image vulnerability scanning, and Kubernetes to schedule many containers. Search for Docker multi-stage builds, GitHub Actions OIDC to a cloud registry, and Kubernetes readiness probes.
